episode_title: What’s Wrong With the Indian Media?

stories.summary: From age six to seventeen, Ajay lived in a housing complex where about 80 households worked in print media, including Hindi, Marathi and Gujarati papers, before television arrived. His father was the second head of the Economic Times Research Bureau (ETRB), which K.A. Antony, formerly of the RBI, had created. Top economists like Hanan Ezekiel edited the Economic Times, and the Times of India grew up around Shamlal and Girilal Jain, whose dense opinion pieces the whole country read. When Ajay was ten, the Emergency came, and the Indian Express ran empty white space rather than print what the censors wanted. Later, Arun Shourie's full-page front-page investigation into A.R. Antulay's trusts cost the Maharashtra chief minister his job. Journalists were poorly paid and the business made little money, but it had a sense of purpose.
stories.insight: Indian journalism as a 'noble calling' is not a myth. Within living memory, newspaper editors had the kind of influence over a nation's thinking that France's philosophers had in the 1960s. Amit adds a caveat: this is partly selective nostalgia, since not everything was rosy then.
stories.quote: It was about being good, valuable participants in the emergence of a good society.

stories.topic: When TV Made the Cricket Match Report Obsolete
stories.summary: When Amit started in cricket journalism in the early 2000s, the job had just changed. A match report used to tell readers what happened. Now readers had already watched the game on TV or knew the result. British papers like The Guardian, the Telegraph and The Times led the shift: ball-by-ball description became a free commodity, so writers had to bring perspective and colour instead. The writing got richer as a result.
stories.insight: This is a small version of journalism's whole crisis of relevance. Once information is abundant, the value moves to perspective and sense-making. Outlets that keep selling the commodity turn into artifacts.
stories.quote: those ball by ball details of this happened, then that happened, then that wicket fell. It was a commodity, it was freely available.

stories.topic: Yahoo India: The Party Photographer vs. the Award-Winning Originals
stories.summary: Around 2009–2010, Prem Panicker ran editorial at Yahoo India (Amit freelanced for him, putting together a columns page). The India team was set a target of 500 million page views a month. Prem built 'Originals', a long-form reporting section with a budget of more than a crore a year; its award-winning pieces drew 40,000–50,000 page views each. Meanwhile a section called OMG, fed by one Bombay photographer paid a one-lakh monthly retainer (12 lakh a year) to shoot Bollywood parties, brought in 450–500 million page views on its own. The higher-ups told Prem his return on investment didn't compare and the money was wasted, and Originals was eventually shut down.
stories.insight: This is the economics behind the gutting of serious journalism. There was no malice involved. A metric that counts every page view the same will always pick party photos over deep reporting.
stories.quote: And at one point he realized that there is one section, which I think was called OMG, which on its own was getting four hundred and fifty million, five hundred million page views a month.

stories.topic: The Editor Whose Job Was to 'Comfort the Comforted'
stories.summary: In the 20th century, journalism took on higher purposes: seeking truth, speaking truth to power, and 'afflicting the comfortable, comforting the afflicted'. Yet the editor of a major Indian newspaper told one of the journalists Amit spoke to that he believed their job was to comfort the comforted. He said it seriously.
stories.insight: Amit calls the statement rational. A newspaper is a business with shareholders, employees and pressure from the state, so inverting journalism's dharma is a response to incentives, not just a personal failing. That is why Amit insists the story has no villains, only structures.
stories.quote: I believe that our job is to comfort the comforted. And he meant it seriously.

stories.summary: In the page-view era, sites split an 800-word piece into four pages of 200 words so that one reader produced four page views. The official justification was the conventional wisdom 'don't make the reader scroll.' As managing editor of Cricinfo, Amit called it bullshit. Cricinfo didn't paginate and avoided pop-ups and other tricks.
stories.insight: An industry 'courtesy' that happens to inflate your own metric is usually a rationalisation. Real respect for readers means good content and as few clicks as possible.
stories.quote: If you give the reader content, she will scroll. If you keep her attention, if you make her interesting, if you give her quality, she will scroll as much as you want her to scroll. It is in fact rude to make the reader click again.

stories.topic: Bennett Coleman's Clickbait Bet That Failed
stories.summary: For a long time the rough rule in Indian media was that Bennett Coleman made money and everyone else together made roughly zero. Ajay then watched the company go all in on tabloidization, scale, lower paper quality and internet clickbait. It had the DNA, size and market punch to win billions of clicks. Its operating profit has nonetheless declined significantly.
stories.insight: If anyone could make a mass-market, advertising-led clickbait model work in India, it was Bennett Coleman. Its failure is a clean natural experiment showing the circle can't be squared. Amit adds that the long-term game being played could never have been won.
stories.quote: So I find it like really the cleanest repudiation of the idea that there is a way to square this circle.

stories.summary: Growing up in the 80s and 90s, Amit thought of journalism as the place where people went if they couldn't get into engineering, medicine or the UPSC. Many old-school journalists he worked with couldn't write a proper English sentence. A noted Hindu journalist, a nice man, once sidled up to him at Chinnaswami Stadium during a cricket match and asked whether 'nevertheless' was two words or three. Amit says we remember the legends, like Arun Shourie, Vir Sanghvi's Sunday magazine, and India Today's copy desk under Dilip Bobb, but they were exceptions.
stories.insight: Nostalgia for a golden age is partly selection bias. Before the internet, readers had no New Yorker or Economist to compare with. Low standards fed low expectations, which fed lower standards.
stories.quote: But these are outliers. This is a selection bias playing out in our memory. We remember the good names.

stories.topic: The New Yorker Fact-Checks One Paragraph
stories.summary: Siddhartha Mukherjee, author of The Emperor of All Maladies, interviewed Ajay over video for a New Yorker article on excess COVID deaths in India; Ajay had one of the first papers on the subject. The magazine's checkers confirmed every sentence attributed to him. That wasn't enough: they asked him to show the paper backing his claims. All this was for one paragraph in a 20,000-word story. T.N. Ninan once told Ajay that quality requires investing in process, meaning enough man-hours at a high enough price per hour. In India, he said, only Bennett Coleman could afford it, and it wouldn't.
stories.insight: Quality journalism comes from expensive process and labour, not talent alone. Indian journalism is chronically under-resourced, produces low quality, and then concludes nobody will pay for it.
stories.quote: Show us the paper. Show us that you have backup for the claims that you made. We'll not take your word for it.

stories.topic: Why Readers Trust the WSJ Against Trump
stories.summary: Trump sued the Wall Street Journal for $10 billion over a recent story. Ajay's reaction was that the WSJ would never make a move like that without being extremely sure of its facts. Trump is famous for suing newspapers, so the paper would have done its hard work before publishing. Readers therefore give it full benefit of the doubt.
stories.insight: A record of rigour lets a paper take on the powerful and keep readers on its side. A media ecosystem without that record has no such reserve of trust to draw on.
stories.quote: It helps that Donald Trump is famous for suing newspapers.

stories.topic: Long-Form Profiles That Were Really Hit Pieces
stories.summary: One Indian magazine known for long-form journalism ran deep profiles that were in fact hit pieces. The writer set out from the start to take the subject down, and most quotes came from unnamed former colleagues. Some of these stories won awards. Amit has read the New Yorker since childhood and found it disgraceful.
stories.insight: Inside a weak ecosystem, awards and prestige reflect that ecosystem's own standards. Readers exposed to a higher benchmark notice the gap at once, and trust erodes.
stories.quote: Most of the quotes would be from unnamed people who would say, I worked with so and so, so and so did this, and that would be the bulk of the story, and stories like that have even won awards.

stories.topic: Sacked Editors and Police at the Door
stories.summary: Amit gave two examples, both from the HT group. When Mint launched, editor Raju Narisetti wrote something that angered P. Chidambaram, who had him sacked; Narisetti left the country. Years later, under the BJP, Bobby Ghosh ran a hate-crime tracker at the Hindustan Times; Arun Jaitley allegedly disliked it and got him sacked. Shephali Bhatt told Amit that after the Financial Times published an exposé of a leading business family, police visited every Indian name on the byline within a day. The foreign lead correspondent went back to her previous posting because of the harassment. Amit also recalled a friend's investigative story, spiked at the last minute, that everyone had admired as explosive. That was exactly why it was spiked.
stories.insight: The state's stick is real, used by both parties, and mostly works through quiet pressure rather than law. It also explains why the small independent outlets, with nothing to lose, are often the ones showing a spine.
stories.quote: A minister in a government has the editor of one of the biggest newspapers in the country summarily sacked, and he left the country.

stories.topic: T.N. Ninan Refuses to Show Columnists Their Views
stories.summary: Around 2006, Ajay asked T.N. Ninan whether he should send columnists data on how many views their pieces got. Ninan said absolutely not. What makes a good editorial or op-ed page should come from the editorial team's own aesthetic and intellectual judgment, built out of their minds and philosophy. Ajay now says he was stupid to ask and Ninan was right. Amit runs his own shows the same way and says he hasn't looked at the figures for The Seen and the Unseen in a year and a half.
stories.insight: Feedback loops built on views slowly replace editorial judgment with whatever the crowd clicks. Refusing to look at the numbers can be a way of protecting the work.
stories.quote: He said this has to be the aesthetic and intellectual judgment of the editorial team, that what's a good editorial page, what's a good op-ed.

stories.summary: About five years ago, a friend who edited the features section of a major publication was carrying a columnist she despised, a misogynist nobody liked. When asked why she kept running him, she said he got more views than everyone else combined.
stories.insight: Once views become the yardstick, they quietly overrule the editor's own taste and values. This is the world Ninan was guarding against.
stories.quote: she said he gets more views than everybody else combined.

stories.summary: Amit wanted to see what the kooky right-wing ecosystem on YouTube looked like. He opened an incognito window, logged into a different Gmail account, and followed the recommendations. He now has two YouTube feeds that have never shown a single common video.
stories.insight: Algorithms don't just bias us; they build separate realities. A newspaper that printed a column for demonetization next to Amit's column against it gave readers a shared world. Without one, people from different feeds will each find the other evil, and from inside their own world that is a reasonable conclusion.
stories.quote: There has never been a common thing that has come up.

stories.topic: Three Physical Papers and a Cup of Coffee
stories.summary: Ajay takes Business Standard, Indian Express and Mint in print. He leaves home by 8:15–8:30 to beat traffic and reads them at the office with coffee. He does it partly for a broad scan of the news, but mostly to get out of his bubble and see the world through editors he respects even when he disagrees with them. He pays attention to page design, photographs articles to send to friends for discussion, and keeps a Google Gemini audio prompt open to ask questions as he reads. He suggests newspapers print a QR code on every story.
stories.insight: A physical paper offers something an algorithm can't: someone else's considered judgment about what matters, built into the layout itself. Here the newspaper works as a deliberate antidote to the filter bubble.
stories.quote: There are priorities embedded in the font size of the headline.

core_ideas.concept: The Crisis of Relevance: Information Is No Longer Scarce
core_ideas.explanation: Journalism is older than newspapers: town criers and oral poets met the needs to know what was happening, to preserve it, and to debate it. Over time it added truth-seeking, sense-making and, in the 20th century, a watchdog role. Its founding reason was that information was scarce, and that is no longer true. Information is abundant, and better sense-makers, often specialists, are everywhere, while the old institutions linger like artifacts. People scrolling Instagram aren't to blame; their needs are being met elsewhere. Ajay pushes back that truth is still scarce, because the information firehose is full of lies from companies, governments and tribes. Amit agrees a good paper should be 'a filter to the truth', but says mainstream media has given up that role.
core_ideas.quote: Today information is abundant. There is practically too much information. It is no longer a scarce resource.

core_ideas.concept: The Partial Outsider
core_ideas.explanation: Janan Ganesh's phrase describes someone who is an outsider to a field but still connected to it. Such a person has influence but isn't bound by the field's conventions, and can apply frameworks from elsewhere. Amit says this position, which he has held in every field he has worked in including journalism, is one of his greatest advantages in understanding the world.
core_ideas.quote: And I think one of my great advantages in understanding the world and in figuring out what I'm doing and finding purpose is I'm a partial outsider to everything that I've been involved in, including journalism.

core_ideas.concept: Dharma vs. Business: The Newsroom as Cost Center
core_ideas.explanation: Every profession has a kind of dharma. Journalism's higher purposes, such as truth-seeking and speaking truth to power, only took shape in the 20th century, while it has always been a business with shareholders and payrolls. Individuals can choose purpose over profit, but a firm has fiduciary duties. Shephali Bhatt's first newsroom treated journalists as a cost centre. Amit treats this as a value-free description of how things are, not an accusation.
core_ideas.quote: Vineet Jain famously said to the New Yorker, we are not in the news business, we are in the advertising business.

core_ideas.concept: Page-View Inflation
core_ideas.explanation: In the 2000s, advertising was the only way to make money online and the page view was the unit being sold. As sites multiplied, page views multiplied, and each became worth less, just as printing money devalues a currency. That pushed publishers into ever more desperate tactics such as clickbait, SEO headlines and pagination, and into a race to the bottom. The metric was also widely gamed.
core_ideas.quote: Now in the same way that in the economy, if you increase the money supply, inflation happens. The value of a rupee goes down. So in a similar sense, the value of a page view goes down.

core_ideas.concept: Platforms Ate the Ad Money, and AI Broke Google's Bargain
core_ideas.explanation: Samarth describes a wave of digital-native outlets from 2010 to 2020, such as Vox, Vice and BuzzFeed. They were promised traffic in exchange for original content, but the advertising money went to Facebook, YouTube and Instagram. Ajay adds a newer blow: Google used to send traffic in return for crawling content, but it now puts a Gemini AI answer at the top of search results, and click-throughs to media sites have collapsed.
core_ideas.quote: So earlier the Faustian bargain that the media sites made with Google was I'll give you free access to crawl my content and you'll bring traffic my way.

core_ideas.concept: Advertising Is Dying; Monetize the Community Directly
core_ideas.explanation: Advertising has always been wasteful. John Wanamaker said half of it is wasted, and Ambi Paramaeswaran says far more than half, and that online ads are a scandal. In the old model a writer sold a piece to a newspaper, which gathered eyeballs, sold them to advertisers and passed the writer a sliver. Readers always valued writers with their time and attention, but writers had no way to capture that value directly. Now they do, through subscriptions, courses and communities, and Amit thinks that for media, advertising is dead.
core_ideas.quote: I don't need the Times of India and I don't need advertisers. I can go directly to my audience and monetize my audience.

core_ideas.concept: Shallow vs. Deep Engagement
core_ideas.explanation: Advertisers treat every page view the same, but a 10-second glance at Bollywood gossip is worth almost nothing, while a 40-minute podcast session is deeply immersive and a host's recommendation carries real credibility. Amit thinks advertisers haven't caught on to this because nobody looks below the surface metric. Every metric can be gamed, but the quality of attention is what actually matters.
core_ideas.quote: I would rather have a hundred thousand downloads of The Seen and the Unseen than twenty million views of a YouTube show

core_ideas.concept: Attributability Shrinks the Imagination
core_ideas.explanation: Digital commerce lets you count exactly which click led to which sale and pay only for that. Ajay first found this appealing, but now thinks it narrows thinking. Building a brand, its visibility and an environment of trust around a business involves much more than whatever can be traced to a click.
core_ideas.quote: But as with so many other fields, this quest for attributability is also shrinking the imagination because it's elementary.

core_ideas.concept: Civic Purpose and the Vanishing Beats
core_ideas.explanation: Samarth's term 'civic purpose' covers beats like the municipality, the RBI, a dusty flyover site or a water problem in one lane. Nobody demands or pays for this coverage, but it records local history. When journalists are treated as cost centres, these beats are cut first and specialists become generalists who file three stories a day. Quality and readership fall, and the cycle feeds itself. Amit doesn't know who will produce this record in the new world, because individual passion can't replace an institution.
core_ideas.quote: You are writing this first draft of history, which will often be the only draft of history.

core_ideas.concept: The Chronic Under-Investment Trap
core_ideas.explanation: Quality comes from process: many well-paid hours behind each well-checked story, as T.N. Ninan told Ajay. Indian journalism is under-resourced and underpaid, so it produces low quality, and the industry then concludes nobody will pay for journalism. Samarth also describes 'invisible quitting': talented people leave one at a time, so it never makes the news. Samarth adds that India's media ecosystem is so shallow that a few failed subscription experiments get read as proof that Indian readers won't pay. Ajay hopes patient investors with hundreds or thousands of crores will fund five years of quality first; Amit is sceptical.
core_ideas.quote: We are under investing in quality and that creates a chronic inability to monetize and then we are stuck.

core_ideas.concept: Gell-Mann Amnesia and the Rise of Specialists
core_ideas.explanation: Michael Crichton named this effect after the physicist Murray Gell-Mann. You read a newspaper story on a subject you know well and see that it's rubbish, then turn the page and trust the rest of the paper. India's generalist journalism makes this especially costly. Since the 2000s, specialists have had their own means of production in blogs and Twitter: Tyler Cowen on economics, Eric Topol on medicine. Readers can see the gap in quality, and they leave.
core_ideas.quote: The idea there being that if they reported your subject wrong, why do you assume they reported everything else right?

core_ideas.concept: Steel-Man the Other Side
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's advice to opinion writers is to state the opposing view so well that an opponent would say 'that's exactly how I would have put it', and only then argue against it. It sharpens your own thinking and shows readers you aren't a partisan hack. Amit says mainstream media rarely does this, as outlets get drawn into narrative battles because outrage brings clicks.
core_ideas.quote: Say it in such a good way that your opponent would say that's exactly how I would have put it, and then argue against it.

core_ideas.concept: The State's Stick and Carrot, and the Inverted Hedge
core_ideas.explanation: In the 1970s and 80s, owners used media to stand up to the state. Ramnath Goenka hired Arun Shourie and spoke truth to power, and the Singhanias started the Indian Post as a hedge during their battle with the Wadias. Today, corporate barons buy media houses to do the government a favour. The stick is pressure on owners' other businesses (an ED raid on a chemical factory, for example), sackings of editors, and police visits. The carrot is government, PSU and party advertising, which can be withdrawn at any time. Small outlets with nothing to lose hold out longest.
core_ideas.quote: You can't hedge against the state. The state is all powerful, the state has too many levers.

core_ideas.concept: Proximity to Government Cheapens the Product
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay points to two more channels of state influence. Media companies earn from conferences, and corporate sponsors come because ministers attend, which gives the government a veto over that income. Newspapers also hand opinion space to sitting civil servants and politicians. The government already has Doordarshan, the PIB and press conferences, so its propaganda is free. Printing it undermines the reason anyone would pay for a newspaper.
core_ideas.quote: Why will I pay a subscription for a newspaper? If you're going to give me Doordarshan.

core_ideas.concept: Price Controls Made TV News Shout
core_ideas.explanation: Ashok Malik's argument, relayed by Amit: in the West, a large share of channel revenue comes from subscriptions, which pays for expensive niche content like National Geographic. In India, channels pay huge licence fees and then face government caps on what they can charge subscribers, so they depend on advertising and race to the bottom. FM radio is similar: high licence fees and a ban on news and politics push every station into mainstream Bollywood, unlike the varied niche stations in New York. The behaviour that looks like private companies failing has regulation at its root.
core_ideas.quote: And his point was it is bad because of government regulation.

core_ideas.concept: Embedded Journalism Comes Home
core_ideas.explanation: Embedded journalism started with reporters travelling with the US Department of Defense in Iraq: the reporter gets access, and coverage tends to go easy on the host. Ajay, citing a friend, says the same arrangement now applies in Kashmir, Naxal-affected districts and parts of the Northeast. The state often blocks independent reporting there, so embedding is the only way in, and the resulting coverage ends up close to PIB and Doordarshan messaging.
core_ideas.quote: so it's back to that damage to the work that comes from proximity to the state.

core_ideas.concept: Social Media Selects for Anger
core_ideas.explanation: Journalists want to go viral, and strong polarised views go viral while plain news doesn't. That erodes the classic separation of news and opinion, and young reporters slip some virtue signalling into news stories. Ajay says that even if no individual chases outrage, the system selects for it. Social media amplifies anger and emotion, views are tallied (he believes Fox News has a live views screen in its newsroom), and so calm reporters lose out while emotional ones get the bonuses.
core_ideas.quote: But more generally we know well that the machine of social media amplifies anger and emotion.

core_ideas.concept: Fragmented Attention and Algorithmic Worlds
core_ideas.explanation: Mornings used to start with a newspaper; now they start with phones, scrolling and swiping. Algorithms feed you more of whatever you clicked. A 15-year-old who clicks one misogynistic, rabble-rousing piece can end up inside a world of that content and take it for reality. A newspaper puts opposing columns on the same page; an algorithm narrows your world to one sliver that may not even be true.
core_ideas.quote: two young people meeting each other is also in a sense two algorithms meeting each other

core_ideas.concept: The Mainstream Is Crumbling, but Nothing Has Replaced It
core_ideas.explanation: The conditions that produced journalism and its values no longer exist, and the mainstream is collapsing in media, entertainment and elsewhere, but institutions lag behind. Solo creators on Substack and YouTube take on parts of the job, especially sense-making. But a reporter covering a city beat can't be expected to also master video, marketing and thumbnails, and once independent, they will start chasing clicks. Ajay says the answer is firms, meaning teams with a business model. So far, the convincing successes globally are old media that reinvented themselves: the FT, the WSJ, the New York Times and The Economist.
core_ideas.quote: But you can't rely on individual passion and drive because that is a few outliers.

core_ideas.concept: Societies Build Immunity to New Media
core_ideas.explanation: This is Suyash Rai's more optimistic account, relayed by Ajay. Every new medium causes damage at first. Radio was a weapon for Mussolini and Hitler: a crackling box urging people to burn the Jews was hugely persuasive. Over time, cultures absorbed radio and normalised it. Today almost nobody takes WhatsApp forwards seriously. Algorithms and social media may follow the same path, but only if culture adapts and people meet each link with scepticism.
core_ideas.quote: The people are not indefinitely stupid. The people are stupid for some time

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit refuses to name the famous journalists' housing enclave where Ajay grew up: 'We won't take the name because we don't want admiring nubile young women to land up at your house if we accidentally give the address away.'

When Amit described himself as a perpetual outsider, Ajay called him 'The mighty podcaster who will not join any club that will have him.' Amit replied: 'I'm really glad, really glad for once that you quoted the right Marx. This of course is Groucho Marx, right? So well done.'

Amit's growing-up view of journalism: it was where society's rejects went, the people who couldn't get into engineering, medicine or the UPSC. One noted Hindu journalist sidled up to him in the Chinnaswami press box and asked, 'Amit, tell me something, is nevertheless two words or three words?'

On the irony of censorship: a friend's investigative story was spiked at the last minute even though everyone said it was explosive ('dhamaka'). As Amit put it, 'But that is the very reason it was sort of spiked.'
After Ajay called the episode plan bleak and asked for something hopeful, Amit says: 'I said we'll do it in the last chapter. I lied.'

Amit on phones: 'I'm not saying everything we do on our phones is wrong. It's only about 99.8% is wrong.' He then goes off on a 'like and subscribe' tangent ('Ajay looks at the numbers. So let's see if my saying this moves the needle... If it does, we'll say it in every episode. No, we won't'), loses his thread, and admits: 'My attention went to hell. See what just happened, these are bad habits.'

After Ajay's ode to reading print with coffee 'like a civilized person', Amit notes that newspapers 'are also useful when you run out of water in the morning and you're stuck in the loo', and predicts the editor will cut it.
Amit interrupts Ajay's vision of media firms full of specialists: 'I just want to interrupt and say no one knows how to make thumbnails. Everybody's winging it.'
Asked how The Seen and the Unseen is doing after going fortnightly, Amit says he hasn't checked the numbers in a year and a half: 'I do the work I do. I'm not a circus monkey.'
Ajay on how far WhatsApp's credibility has fallen: 'Today, like everybody knows WhatsApp is bullshit... I mean, IIT Bombay 1987 group. I don't take it that seriously.'

When Ajay recommends Roger Waters' Amused to Death, Amit says he's 'just piggybacking on words.' Ajay explains that Waters read the Postman book before writing it. Asked if he made that up, he says: 'No no seriously I'm not just an LLM.'
Thucydides, the ancient historian Amit says is often called the first journalist because of how rigorously he verified his sources.
Napster, recalled as the era when people expected digital content, music included, to be free, which left advertising as the only way to make money online.

John Wanamaker's line that half the money spent on advertising is wasted and nobody knows which half. Ambi Paramaeswaran told Amit it's much more than half, and that what advertisers do online is a scandal that simply isn't working.
L.K. Advani on the press during the Emergency: 'they were asked to bend, they chose to crawl', set against Ramnath Goenka's blank page in the Indian Express.

'If you ain't got nothing, you got nothing to lose', quoted by Amit, who wasn't sure whether it came from Dylan, Joan Baez or Kris Kristofferson, to explain why small independent outlets are the ones showing a spine.

Hanan Ezekiel, 'brother of the much more famous Nissim Ezekiel, but really one of the best economists of India', once edited the Economic Times. Ajay compares that era's editors to France's 1960s philosophers.
Prem Panicker's verdict, quoted by Amit: the Indian media is 'a mile wide and an inch deep'.
The classic journalistic motto 'afflict the comfortable, comfort the afflicted', and journalism as 'the first draft of history', which Amit extends to 'often the only draft of history'.
